thread.title: New York Fashion Week: How a new app could economically transform the fashion industry

title: New York Fashion Week: How a new app could economically transform the fashion industry
text:
Published: Feb 14, 2018 11:11 a.m. ET Share 
Badgley Mischka show attendees use app to respond to runway styles in real time Ilya S. Savenok/Getty Images for IMG The most ‘loved’ dress as voted by users of an app during Badgley Mischka’s NYFW show. 
By Entertainment writer 
Design duo Mark Badgley and James Mischka make for unlikely tech visionaries. 
The designer business Badgley Mischka, which has been going strong for three decades, is renown for its beaded gowns and was recently saluted by Vogue.com for catering to clientele who hark back to “when being a part of high society—or dressing like you were—was a much more important mark of status than the number of Instagram followers you have.” 
Yet in what marked the first initiative of its kind in the fashion business, attendees at their fall 2018 show at New York Fashion Week were encouraged to download an app, powered by global software provider SAP SAP, +1.16% that rated the look of each Badgley Mischka outfit appearing on the runway in front of them. 
The app, via the aid of beacon technology, quizzed users on whether they “liked” or “loved” each look they saw and supplied information on each garment. 
179 users from 17 different countries cast 1,396 votes on Badgley Mischka clothes during the 15-minute show. Badgley and Mischka were watching the interactive feedback on an iPad while the show was in progress. Afterward, the information went public for users who weren’t in the room. SAP The Badgley Mischka/ SAP app 
“I was surprised by the results which makes it even more fascinating,” Mark Badgley told MarketWatch. The outfit that received the most “love” votes was a crimson ballgown. A short black dress also proved popular. 
“I’m probably the lowest tech guy you could ever meet in your entire life,” Badgley said, “but for all the millennials out there and the way the world’s changing, I find it amusing that probably the most classic old school type of ballgown still reigns supreme.” 
He added: “It just goes to show you that some things are true and everlasting. I love the fact that that ball gown was everyone’s favorite because it’s very true to our brand. It didn’t have to be some crazy avant-garde piece that came out of the runway that was the favorite.” 
“People who were at the show are the decision-makers in the fashion industry — the buyers, the press, the bloggers,” said James Mischka. “[They are] the people who really do have a voice. We get to hear from them right now, what they think, instead of waiting for six months from now when we get the final feedback from the retailers.” 
For the designers, this went beyond attempting to increase its credibility with a younger crowd. The instantaneous response on what proved popular will enable the company to manage its inventory better, operate faster and make its fall collection more cost-efficient. 
“The information we’re getting from it is for our sales and production team,” said Mischka. “We’re still going to design what we want to design and we obviously listen to our clients and our market but at the same time this is going to streamline the sales process and the production process for our company.” 
Lori Mitchell-Keller, global general manager for consumer industries at SAP, said the partnership has its origins in her company’s software user collaboration with Apple AAPL, +0.60% . 
“What brought us to Badgley Mischka was that they were also trying to figure out how they get products to consumers faster than they’ve been able to do and how to integrate more technology into their business,” she said. “They’re really trying to appeal at a price point that’s a little bit lower than some of the couture fashion houses so it attracts some of the younger buyers who want to interact with technology.” 
Badgley Mischka’s tech initiative comes as social media platforms have revolutionized fashion and the “See Now, Buy Now” model that, for the last two years, has disrupted the traditional six-month wait between the runway and when the clothes arrive in stores. 
Coco Rocha, the Canadian model who has sometimes been referred to as the world’s first digital supermodel for her pioneering use of tech platforms, joined Badgley and Mischka at a talk after their show entitled “Demystifying Digital,” together with Jen Morgan, executive board member, global customer operations, SAP North America. Ilya S. Savenok/Getty Images for IMG The ‘Demystifying Digital’ panel 
Rocha said the fashion industry has been slow to embrace tech. “It’s an industry that always thought it was ahead of the times in everything,” she said, “but for tech it was never ahead of the times. They were slow thinking about it and got scared. But they’re going to come to realize that there is a lot of useful tech they can use.” 
She added: “This isn’t our grandpa and grandma’s generation anymore where we hem and haw about stuff. Fashion kids can tell immediately if they like something or not.” 
Rocha thought the app marked an economically significant moment in fashion. “Usually if their clothes don’t sell, the designers have to buy back their clothing and that’s a huge debt to them,” she said. “So you’re saving time and money with an easy app for people to use. If everyone uses this app, they will save a lot of money in their own companies.” 
She also viewed the fashion week runway app as a throwback. “It’s funny how we’re going forward but we’re actually going backwards at the same time,” Rocha said. “A hundred years ago a tailor would make a suit exactly to my body. It was all about how it would look great ‘just for me.’ We’re going back to that using technology.” 
“There was huge uptake for the app — the vast majority of people at the show were using it,” said SAP’s Mitchell-Keller. “This is just the tip of the iceberg. There are a lot of other things we could do with this app in terms of allowing customers to make comments and allowing buyers to actually place an order.” 
She added: “I know that IMG [the entertainment and sports management company which operates fashion week] wants to sit down with us and many of the designers and work out how can we can potentially do something similar for other designers. I think it’s just the beginning.” More from MarketWatch
